summary: AE + SE walked Bluehaven through Redwood SDK quickstarts for Python and TypeScript; covered auth via REDWOOD_API_KEY, env setup, streaming, and Console Optimize basics. Customer requested pilot bench, security docs, and a trial org/API key.
topics: Next steps: trial org and bench run
transcript: [00:00] Nora: Hi everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Nora from Redwood, I'll run today's quickstart. Samir and Jamie are with me. Can you hear us okay?
[00:08] Lina: Yes, loud and clear. Thanks, Nora. We have about 45 minutes; main goal is to get our engineers unblocked on the SDK and auth flow.
[00:16] Samir: Great, we'll cover Python and TypeScript snippets, env patterns, and then a Console tour focusing on Optimize. There will be some perf notes too.
[00:25] Tom: Quick ask up front — we want streaming tokens into our realtime service. So more interested in latency/streaming patterns than batch embeddings right now.
[00:33] Jamie: Noted. We'll show streaming in Node and async generator style in Python. Ok starting with install — Python pip install redwood-inference, npm i @redwood/inference for TS.

[01:05] Samir: For auth the simplest pattern is REDWOOD_API_KEY as an env var; in prod you can swap that for a secret manager reference or inject via your runtime. Example: export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-xxxxx
[01:28] Ethan: Do you recommend storing it in AWS Secrets Manager or in K8s secrets?
[01:34] Jamie: Both are fine; for Bluehaven we usually suggest KMS-backed secrets store. We support customer-managed keys — you can bring your own KMS for Private deployments.
[01:50] Reema: Is the key single-tenant? we need audit logs and rotation policy for SOC 2 compliance.
[01:56] Nora: Yes, Dedicated and Private tiers give isolated pools and full audit logs. We'll attach our security pack after the call with details on rotation, SSO, and audit trails.

[02:10] Samir: Switching to code — Python quickstart. I'll paste the snippet: from redwood import RedwoodClient; client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.environ['REDWOOD_API_KEY']); resp = client.generate('Summarize the latest sales notes'); print(resp.text)
[02:45] Tom: Slight nit — our service uses asyncio extensively. Is there an async client?
[02:51] Samir: Yep, there's AsyncRedwoodClient; sample: async with AsyncRedwoodClient() as client: async for token in client.stream('...'): process(token)
[03:09] Lina: Any rate limits we should be aware of on trial orgs?
[03:14] Nora: Trial orgs have conservative quotas to prevent abuse but enough for small benches; we'll lift quotas for the pilot bench Samir will run if you sign the NDA.

[03:30] Jamie: Now TypeScript example — const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); const stream = client.streamCompletion({model: 'gptx-lite', prompt: '…'}); for await (const chunk of stream) { console.log(chunk.text) }
[04:05] Ethan: What's the preferred Node runtime? we're on Node 18 in production.
[04:10] Jamie: Node 16+ works fine; streaming uses async iterators so Node 18 is perfect. Also, there are small helpers in the SDK for reconnect and backpressure handling.
[04:35] Tom: How do we wire up tracing? We use Datadog and Jaeger for request traces.
[04:41] Samir: Console exposes per-request IDs in response headers; you can propagate those. We also have integrations for common tracing libs — we'll share the tracing hook doc.
[05:02] Reema: On network: if we go VPC/private, how does egress work? we need to avoid internet egress from certain hosts.
[05:09] Nora: For Private we can do VPC peering and private endpoints — no public egress required. We'll add VPC docs to the security packet.
[05:22] Lina: Back to SDK: any gotchas on long responses and KV cache? We have multi-turn conversations and want to reuse the KV cache efficiently.

[05:31] Samir: Current runtime supports prefix KV cache — the SDK exposes a cache_key param. One caveat: if you stream partial tokens and close early, you need to flush the cache explicitly, small footgun but documented.
[06:00] Tom: Could you repeat that flush pattern?
[06:05] Samir: Sure — client.cache.flush(cache_key) after confirm of generation. The SDK also has automatic TTLs to avoid stale states.
[06:22] Ethan: On cost — do you have a per-token estimate for the gptx-lite model?

[06:28] Nora: We'll send a pricing sheet but rough publicly: hosted gptx-lite is cheaper than gptx-large; Optimize will recommend quantized variants and batching for cost wins. Exact numbers in the pricing pack.

[06:45] Jamie: Quick Console tour: logging into Console you can see per-route token cost, latency p95, and route-specific rollouts. Optimize tab surfaces batching and quantization suggestions by workload.
[07:05] Lina: Can we pin model versions in the Console? We need deterministic behavior for production.
[07:09] Jamie: Yes — model pins, canary, and A/B are supported. You can also set fallback policies if capacity constrained.
[07:25] Reema: For encryption at rest, do you support customer-managed keys (CMK)?
[07:29] Nora: Yes — CMK for Dedicated and Private; hosted has provider-managed keys but we can discuss hybrid options for enterprise.
[07:50] Tom: Let's do a quick live run — Ethan, can you share your screen with a terminal?
[07:56] Ethan: Yep sharing now...

[08:15] Samir: I'll paste a short Python async streaming example. (typing sounds) async with AsyncRedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')) as client: async for chunk in client.stream('Explain event-sourcing in 2 sentences'): print(chunk.text)
[08:47] Ethan: That printed tokens in chunks, nice. How does reconnect work if we have flaky lambda cold starts?

[08:54] Jamie: SDK has an auto-reconnect with exponential backoff and an onResume token offset so you don't re-generate from scratch. But there is a slight duplication risk, handle idempotency at application level.
[09:20] Lina: Any advice on batching for low-latency setups? we care about p50 under 200ms ideally.
[09:26] Samir: For strict latency SLOs avoid long batching windows. Use small continuous batching (millisecond-level) and prefix cache. Also choose smaller model family or p-tune to reduce tokens.
[09:50] Tom: Does the SDK surface token-level cost before the request completes? we want to estimate cost for a given prompt before sending bulk jobs.
[09:57] Jamie: There's an estimateCost API that returns token projections — it's not exact but good for budgeting. Console also shows historical per-route cost.
[10:15] Reema: Security question — SAML SSO for Console? our org requires SAML and SCIM provisioning.
[10:21] Nora: We support SAML SSO and SCIM for user provisioning. We'll include our SSO integration guide in the follow-up.
[10:40] Lina: Back on integration — do you have sample Helm charts or K8s manifests for sidecar patterns?
[10:47] Samir: We have example manifests in the repo — sidecar for secret injection plus a small wrapper for rotating API keys. We'll link that.
[11:05] Ethan: We also use TypeScript serverless functions. Is there a recommended pattern for streaming into edge functions?
[11:11] Jamie: For edge, use small token windows and short-lived connections — it's supported but be careful with cold starts, prewarm where possible.
[11:35] Tom: Can we set model fallbacks per route? if our primary model is down, we'd like an automatic degrade to a cheaper model.
[11:41] Nora: Yes, route-level fallback policies support model maps and region fallback. You can set cost vs latency priorities.
[12:00] Samir: Quick demo of Optimize: here it recommends quantizing to int8 for this workload and suggests a batching window of 30ms — projected 38% cost decrease with p95 latency impact of +5ms.
[12:25] Lina: Nice. Is the quantized model API-compatible or do we need code changes?
[12:30] Samir: API-compatible — model name changes but endpoints and parameters stay the same. We recommend a test pass to validate quality.
[12:50] Reema: If we use Private (on-prem), how do updates to the runtime happen? air-gapped constraints matter.
[12:56] Nora: For air-gapped we ship a controlled bundle and provide upgrade tooling. There's a documented process for validation before applying updates.
[13:20] Ethan: One more quick dev question — where's the official SDK repo?
[13:24] Jamie: github.com/redwood-inference/sdk — we'll send direct links. Also a Quickstart notebook link: https://console.redwood.ai/quickstarts/bluehaven-notebook
[13:40] Tom: Ok we're about halfway; any items we should prioritize for the pilot?
[13:45] Lina: Perf on our streamed conversational workload, security review (SOC 2 + KMS), and a clean TypeScript example for our serverless pipeline.
[13:55] Nora: Great, Samir will set up the bench and provide template data ingestion script. We'll also provision a trial org for Ethan to try samples.
[14:12] Samir: I'll also include a perf script that runs parallel streaming clients and captures p50/p95 and token costs, along with a small harness for KV cache testing.

[14:32] Jamie: Back to code — a brief note on error handling: SDK raises typed exceptions like RedwoodRateLimitError and RedwoodTimeoutError; you should catch and implement exponential backoff + jitter.
[14:50] Ethan: Does the SDK expose request ids in exceptions for tracing?
[14:54] Samir: Yes, exceptions include request_id and x-redwood-request headers so you can correlate logs.
[15:10] Reema: Can we get SIEM integration? we forward logs to Splunk.
[15:15] Nora: We provide log forwarding options and CloudTrail-style audit exports for Dedicated/Private. We'll include Splunk hints in the security packet.
[15:30] Tom: Any limitations on streaming concurrency per API key?
[15:35] Nora: Trial keys lower concurrency; Dedicated contracts specify higher concurrency and throughput caps. We'll surface exact numbers in the contract deck.

[15:50] Samir: Quick flesh-out of a TypeScript streaming handler: (shows code) const res = await client.completions.stream({model, prompt}); for await (const event of res) { if (event.type === 'delta') pushToSocket(event.delta) }
[16:15] Ethan: That's exactly what we need for websocket proxying. One question: can we preempt or cancel an in-flight generation?
[16:21] Jamie: You can send a cancel request referencing request_id and the server will stop generation; the SDK exposes client.cancel(request_id).
[16:40] Lina: Let's circle security: audit logs retention — what's default and can we extend it?
[16:45] Nora: Default retention varies by plan; enterprise add-on extends retention up to multi-year. We'll include retention table in follow-up.
[17:02] Tom: For the pilot, we'll likely want a week-long bench across our dev corpus. Can you recommend sample sizes?
[17:08] Samir: For meaningful p95 numbers include at least 5k NLU requests with typical context lengths. We'll provide ingestion script.
[17:30] Jamie: One subtlety — if you use prefix caching aggressively, ensure prompt canonicalization so cache keys align across producers.
[17:45] Ethan: Good point; we have multiple microservices generating similar prompts with small token differences.
[17:52] Samir: We'll show canonicalization helper functions in the repo.
[18:10] Nora: Time check — about 30 minutes left. Any blockers to proceed with a pilot?
[18:16] Lina: Nope, just need the security pack and the trial org. Also want an estimated cost for our 100k token/day baseline.
[18:26] Nora: We'll include a cost projection in the pricing sheet; Samir will run a quick estimator with your profile.
[18:40] Tom: Can Redwood run a small A/B on our production traffic? we'd like to compare answers against current model.
[18:46] Nora: We can support shadowing mode and A/B with minimal latency impact. We'll propose the rollout plan in the follow-up.
[19:05] Jamie: One final code tip — for local dev set REDWOOD_API_KEY in .env and use the SDK dev proxy to replay responses. That reduces need for live calls during unit tests.
[19:20] Ethan: Nice. Could you share an example .env and docker-compose dev setup?
[19:25] Samir: Yep will add to the repo and notebook.
[19:40] Reema: Ok I'm skimming the console — how granular are RBAC roles? we want least-privilege for deploy and ops.
[19:46] Nora: RBAC supports route-level and org-level roles, and we integrate with SCIM group mappings. Details in security doc.
[20:05] Lina: Quick question on tokenization differences across models — do you expose token counts before generation?
[20:10] Jamie: There's a tokenizer tool in SDK that mirrors the runtime tokenizer; use client.tokenize(prompt) to get counts client-side.
[20:30] Tom: Cool. We're at ~30 minutes in — maybe wrap with explicit next steps.

[20:36] Nora: Sure recap: Nora share quickstart notebook + links, Samir schedule pilot bench and perf script, Samir + Jamie include dev manifests and canonicalization helpers, Nora share security pack and trial org credentials for Ethan.
[20:55] Lina: Sounds good. I'll coordinate internally and send the NDA to Nora if needed.
[21:05] Nora: Perfect. Any final quick clarifications?
[21:12] Ethan: One last: where do we raise infra tickets for Private deployment?
[21:17] Nora: We'll route through our solutions team; I'll cc the deployment lead in the follow-up thread.
[21:30] Tom: Thanks all — this was helpful. We'll pick up after you send the materials.
[21:36] Nora: Thanks everyone — end of recording.
